beats.say: We want the average of these five numbers: 44, 26, 51, 56, 48.
Think of the average as levelling out. We pile everything together, then give each number the same share.
First the total. We add one number at a time. 44 plus 26 is 70. Add 51 to get 121.
Keep going. Add 56 to get 177, and 48 more makes 225.
The total is 225. Now, what do we divide it by?

ask.ifNot: Count the numbers in the list. There are 5 of them, so the total is shared 5 ways.

beats.say: 225 divided by 5 is 45, because 5 times 45 is 225.
So the average is 45.
Does it look sensible? The smallest number is 26 and the biggest is 56, and 45 sits between them. An average always does.
Two steps every time: find the total, then share it by the count.
The average of 4 numbers is 58. We know 3 of them: 71, 56, 72. We must find the missing one.
An average is a fair share. It is as if every one of the 4 numbers were 58. That tells us the total.
So how do we find the total of all 4 numbers?

ask.ifNot: If each of the 4 numbers were 58, the total would be 4 lots of 58. So we multiply.

beats.say: 58 times 4 is 232. All 4 numbers together make 232.
Now add the 3 numbers we know. 71 plus 56 is 127, and 72 more makes 199.
The missing number is whatever is left. 232 minus 199 is 33.
The missing number is 33.
Check: 199 plus 33 is 232, and 232 divided by 4 is 58. It works.
Turn the average into a total first. The missing number is the total minus the rest.
The average of 4 numbers is 49. Then a new number, 59, joins them. What is the new average?

board.text: Average of 4 numbers is 49. A new number 59 joins.

beats.say: We do not know what the 4 numbers are. But we do not need to! Their total is enough.
4 numbers with an average of 49 add up to the same as 4 lots of 49. 49 times 4 is 196.
Now the new number joins the pot. 196 plus 59 is 255.
We must share the new total. How many numbers are there now?

ask.ifNot: There were 4 numbers, and 1 more joined. 4 plus 1 is 5. Forgetting to count the new one is the classic slip.

beats.say: There are 5 numbers now. 255 divided by 5 is 51, because 5 times 51 is 255.
The new average is 51.
The new number, 59, is bigger than the old average, 49. So it pulled the average up a little. That makes sense.
Go through the total every time. Find it, add the new number, and share it among one more.
Rohit's runs in five cricket matches were 34, 52, 47, 25 and 43. In which match did he score the most runs?
Most runs means the biggest number. To compare numbers with two digits, look at the tens digit first.
Which of these numbers has the biggest tens digit?

ask.ifNot: The tens digits are 3, 5, 4, 2 and 4. The biggest is 5, and that belongs to 52.

beats.say: 52 has 5 tens. No other score has that many, so 52 is the biggest.
Now look back at the table. Which match has 52 runs? It is Match 2.
Rohit scored the most runs in Match 2.
Careful: the answer is the match, not the number of runs. Find the biggest number, then read off its label.
Each picture of a book stands for 5 books sold. Monday has 4 pictures, Tuesday 6, Wednesday 3 and Thursday 5. On which day were the fewest books sold?

board.text: Each picture = 5 books. Fewest books on which day?

spec.note: Each picture stands for 5 books

beats.say: Here are the pictures for each day.
Do we need to work out the number of books for every day?

ask.ifNot: Every picture stands for the same number of books. So the day with the fewest pictures also has the fewest books.

beats.say: Every picture is worth the same. So fewer pictures means fewer books. We only need the smallest number of pictures.
Of 4, 6, 3 and 5, the smallest is 3. That is Wednesday.
Let's check with books. Wednesday's 3 pictures make 15 books. Monday's 4 pictures make 20, which is more.
The fewest books were sold on Wednesday.
Read the word carefully. Fewest means the smallest, not the biggest.
In a tally chart, each bundle stands for 5 and each single stroke stands for 1. The row for parrots has 3 bundles and 2 single strokes. How many parrots?

spec.note: A bundle stands for 5, a single stroke for 1

beats.say: A tally bundle is four strokes with one more drawn across them. That is why a bundle always stands for 5.
So what are 3 bundles worth?

ask.ifNot: Each bundle stands for 5. 3 bundles are 3 lots of 5, and 3 times 5 is 15.

beats.say: 3 times 5 is 15. Or just count in fives: 5, 10, 15.
Now the 2 single strokes. Each one is worth 1, so we add 2. 15 plus 2 is 17.
17 parrots were counted.
Count the bundles in fives, then count on the single strokes.
The children present in Class 4 were: Monday 38, Tuesday 35, Wednesday 40, Thursday 32. How many more children were present on Wednesday than on Tuesday?

board.text: How many more on Wednesday than on Tuesday?

spec.note: How many more on Wednesday than on Tuesday?

beats.say: The table has four days, but we only need two of them. Pick out Wednesday and Tuesday.
We want to know how many more. Which sum finds that?

ask.ifNot: How many more means the gap between the two numbers. To find a gap, take the smaller from the bigger: 40 minus 35.

beats.say: 40 minus 35 is 5.
5 more children were present on Wednesday.
Check by counting up: 35 and 5 more makes 40. Yes.
Two tips: use only the rows the question asks about, and for how many more, subtract.
A bar graph shows samosas sold: Monday 12, Tuesday 15, Wednesday 9, Thursday 15, Friday 11. Which two days have bars of the same height?

board.text: Which two days have bars of the same height?

spec.note: Which two bars have the same height?

beats.say: In a bar graph, the height of a bar shows its number. So equal bars mean equal numbers.
Look along the numbers. Which number appears twice?

ask.ifNot: Read them slowly: 12, 15, 9, 15, 11. The 15 comes up two times.

beats.say: 15 appears twice: once for Tuesday and once for Thursday.
12 and 11 are close, but close is not equal. Those two bars would be a little different.
The bars of the same height are Tuesday and Thursday.
To find equal bars, hunt for a number that shows up twice.
The children of Class 4 each chose one favourite fruit: Mango 14, Banana 6, Apple 9, Guava 5. How many children chose banana or guava?

board.text: How many chose banana or guava?

beats.say: There are four fruits in the table, but the question only asks about two. Banana has 6 children, and guava has 5.
Banana or guava means everyone in either group. So what do we do with 6 and 5?

ask.ifNot: We want the two groups together. Putting groups together means adding.

beats.say: 6 plus 5 is 11.
11 children chose banana or guava.
Each child chose just one fruit, so nobody is counted twice. Pick the rows you need, then add.
Six children got these marks in a spelling test: 14, 18, 9, 20, 12, 17. How many children got more than 15 marks?

board.text: Marks: 14, 18, 9, 20, 12, 17. How many are more than 15?

spec.note: How many marks are more than 15?

beats.say: We check each mark against 15, one at a time. A ring if it is more than 15, and a line through it if not.
14 is less than 15, so cross it out. 18 is more, so ring it. 9 is less, cross it out.
Now 20, 12 and 17. Which of these are more than 15?

ask.ifNot: 20 is more than 15, and so is 17. But 12 is less than 15, so it does not count.

beats.say: 20, ring. 12, cross it out. 17, ring.
Count the rings: 18, 20 and 17. That is 3 children.
Notice that 14 is close to 15, but it is still less, so it does not count.
Go through the list one by one and mark each number. Then count your rings.
Each child in a class chose one favourite game: Cricket 13, Kho-kho 8, Football 7, Carrom 4. How many children are in the class?

spec.note: How many children are in the class?

beats.say: Each child chose one game. How do we find the number of children in the class?

ask.ifNot: Every child is in exactly one of the four groups. So the class is all four groups put together. We add.

beats.say: Let's add smartly. Look for pairs that make a round number. 13 and 7 make 20.
And 8 and 4 make 12.
20 plus 12 is 32.
There are 32 children in the class.
When you add a list, pair up numbers that make tens. It is quicker and safer.
In a tally chart, a bundle stands for 5 and a single stroke stands for 1. Which of the choices shows 23?
Bundles are fives. So we ask how many fives fit into 23. Count in fives: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25.
How many bundles can we use without going past 23?

ask.ifNot: 5 bundles make 25, which is already more than 23. 4 bundles make 20, and that fits.

beats.say: 4 bundles make 20. That is as close as fives can get.
From 20 up to 23 we need 3 more. Those are 3 single strokes.
So 23 is shown by 4 bundles and 3 strokes.
Careful: 2 bundles and 3 strokes just copies the digits of 23. But 2 bundles are only 10, so that shows 13.
Take out as many fives as you can. What is left is the single strokes.
Each picture of a sun stands for 2 sunny days. January has 5 pictures, February 8, March 6 and April 9. Which month had 16 sunny days?

board.text: Each sun = 2 sunny days. Which month had 16?

spec.note: Each picture stands for 2 sunny days

beats.say: We could work out the days for every month. But here is a shortcut: work backwards from the 16.
Each picture stands for 2 days. How many pictures make 16 days?

ask.ifNot: We are asking how many 2s fit into 16. 16 divided by 2 is 8.

beats.say: 16 divided by 2 is 8. So we need 8 pictures.
Now look for the month with 8 pictures. That is February.
February had 16 sunny days.
Check: 8 times 2 is 16. Yes. When a question gives you the total, divide to get back to the pictures.
The heights of five plants in centimetres are: Rose 34, Tulsi 28, Neem 41, Mint 19, Lily 37. Which plant is the second tallest?
Second tallest means: find the tallest, set it aside, and then find the tallest of the rest.
First, which plant is the tallest?

ask.ifNot: Look at the tens digits. Only 41 has 4 tens, so Neem is the tallest.

beats.say: Neem is the tallest at 41. But that is not what we were asked! Set it aside.
Now the rest: 34, 28, 19 and 37. Two of them have 3 tens: 34 and 37. Compare the ones. 7 is more than 4, so 37 wins.
The second tallest plant is Lily.
In order from the tallest, the heights are 41, 37, 34, 28, 19. Lily is second.
For second biggest, find the biggest first, cross it out, then look again.
The side of a bar graph is marked 0, 10, 20, 30, 40. Tuesday's bar ends exactly halfway between 20 and 30. What number does it show?

board.text: The bar ends halfway between 20 and 30. It shows ?

spec.note: Tuesday's bar ends exactly halfway between 20 and 30

beats.say: The bar goes up past 20, but it does not reach 30. So the answer is somewhere between them.
How far apart are the two marks? 30 minus 20 is 10.
The bar stops halfway across that gap of 10. What is half of 10?

ask.ifNot: Half means two equal parts. 10 split into two equal parts gives 5 and 5.

beats.say: Half of 10 is 5. So the bar ends 5 above the 20 mark. 20 plus 5 is 25.
Tuesday's bar shows 25.
Check: 25 is 5 above 20 and 5 below 30. Right in the middle.
When a bar ends between two marks, find the gap, then work out how far across it the bar goes.
In a pictograph, each picture stands for 3 kites. Ravi's row has 5 pictures and Meena's row has 8 pictures. How many more kites does Meena have than Ravi?

board.text: 1 picture = 3 kites. Ravi 5 pictures, Meena 8 pictures.
How many more kites does Meena have?

spec.note: Each picture stands for 3 kites

beats.say: Let's compare the pictures first. Meena has 8 and Ravi has 5. 8 minus 5 is 3, so Meena has 3 more pictures.
Is 3 the answer?

ask.ifNot: The question asks for kites. 3 is the number of extra pictures, and each picture stands for 3 kites.

beats.say: Each extra picture is worth 3 kites. 3 times 3 is 9.
Meena has 9 more kites than Ravi.
Check the long way. Meena has 8 times 3, which is 24 kites. Ravi has 5 times 3, which is 15. And 24 minus 15 is 9.
In a pictograph, always change pictures into the real thing before you answer.
In a pictograph of library books, each picture stands for 5 books. Monday has 4 pictures, Tuesday has 6 and Wednesday has 3. How many books were borrowed altogether?

board.text: 1 picture = 5 books. Mon 4, Tue 6, Wed 3 pictures.

spec.note: Each picture stands for 5 books

beats.say: Every picture is worth the same. So we can count all the pictures first, and change them into books at the end.
4 plus 6 plus 3 is 13 pictures.
13 pictures, and each one stands for 5 books. What do we do now?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 13 pictures stands for 5 books. 13 lots of 5 means we multiply.

beats.say: 13 times 5. 10 fives are 50, and 3 fives are 15. 50 plus 15 is 65.
65 books were borrowed altogether.
Check day by day: 20 books, 30 books and 15 books. 20 plus 30 plus 15 is 65.
13 is only the number of pictures. Always turn the pictures into books.
Each picture stands for 6 eggs. A farmer's chart has 5 pictures for Monday and 3 for Tuesday. He packs all these eggs in boxes of 12. How many boxes does he fill?

spec.note: Each picture stands for 6 eggs. A box holds 12 eggs

beats.say: This has three steps: pictures, then eggs, then boxes. We take them one at a time.
Pictures first. 5 plus 3 is 8 pictures.
Each picture is 6 eggs. 8 times 6 is 48 eggs.
48 eggs go into boxes of 12. How do we find the number of boxes?

ask.ifNot: We are asking how many 12s fit into 48. That is a division.

beats.say: Count in twelves: 12, 24, 36, 48. That is 4 twelves. So 48 divided by 12 is 4.
The farmer fills 4 boxes.
A neat shortcut: 2 pictures make 12 eggs, which is 1 box. So 8 pictures fill 4 boxes.
Do not stop at 8 pictures or at 48 eggs. Keep going until you reach what the question asks for.
A sweet shop sold 60 laddoos in four days: Monday 12, Tuesday 18, Thursday 14. The number for Wednesday is smudged. How many were sold on Wednesday?
The whole is 60. Three parts are known and one is hidden. So first find what the three known parts add up to.
12 and 18 make a round 30. Then 14 more makes 44.
The three known days make 44, and the total is 60. How do we find Wednesday?

ask.ifNot: The 60 already holds all four days. Take away the three we know, and Wednesday is what is left.

beats.say: 60 minus 44 is 16.
16 laddoos were sold on Wednesday.
Check: 12 plus 18 plus 16 plus 14 is 60. It fits.
The missing part is the whole, minus the parts you know.
Tickets sold at a mela: on Saturday, 20 adult and 35 child tickets. On Sunday, 28 adult and 30 child tickets. How many more tickets were sold on Sunday than on Saturday?

board.text: Sat: 20 adult, 35 child.   Sun: 28 adult, 30 child.
How many more tickets on Sunday?

spec.note: How many more tickets on Sunday than on Saturday?

beats.say: The question says tickets, and that means all tickets, adult and child together. So we need each day's total first.
Saturday: 20 plus 35 is 55.
Sunday: 28 plus 30 is 58.
Saturday has 55 and Sunday has 58. How many more on Sunday?

ask.ifNot: Take Saturday's total away from Sunday's. 58 minus 55 is 3.

beats.say: 58 minus 55 is 3. So 3 more tickets were sold on Sunday.
The trap is to compare only the adult tickets, 28 and 20. That leaves out the children. Total each day first, then compare.
In a pictograph, each picture stands for 4 children, and Monday's row has 6 pictures. The chart is drawn again with each picture standing for 8 children. How many pictures now?

board.text: Drawn again with 1 picture = 8 children. Pictures = ?

spec.note: Each picture stands for 4 children. Now each must stand for 8

beats.say: The pictures change, but the children do not! So first find how many children there really are.
6 pictures of 4 children each. 6 times 4 is 24 children.
Now each picture stands for 8 children. Will we need more pictures, or fewer?

ask.ifNot: Each new picture holds more children than before. So fewer pictures are needed to show the same 24 children.

beats.say: How many 8s fit into 24? Count: 8, 16, 24. That is 3.
Monday's row will have 3 pictures.
Notice: each picture is now worth twice as much, so we need half as many. Half of 6 is 3.
When the key of a pictograph changes, go back to the real number first.
A full picture stands for 10 coconuts and a half picture for 5. Monday's row has 3 full pictures and 1 half picture. Tuesday's row has 2 full pictures. How many coconuts in all?

board.text: Monday: 3 full and 1 half.    Tuesday: 2 full.

spec.note: Full picture 10 coconuts, half picture 5. Total = ?

beats.say: Monday first. 3 full pictures are 3 times 10, which is 30.
Monday also has a half picture. What do we add for it?

ask.ifNot: A half picture stands for half of 10 coconuts, and that is 5.

beats.say: 30 plus 5 is 35 coconuts on Monday.
Tuesday: 2 full pictures are 2 times 10, which is 20.
Both days together: 35 plus 20 is 55.
55 coconuts were sold on the two days.
A half picture counts for half. Work out each row, then add.
A tally chart of birds uses bundles of 5 and single strokes. Crows: 2 bundles and 3 strokes. Sparrows: 3 bundles and 1 stroke. Pigeons: 1 bundle and 4 strokes. How many birds in all?

board.text: Crows: 2 bundles 3 strokes.  Sparrows: 3 bundles 1 stroke.

spec.note: A bundle is 5, a stroke is 1. How many birds in all?

beats.say: Each bundle is 5 and each stroke is 1. We do one bird at a time. Crows: 2 fives are 10, plus 3 is 13.
Sparrows have 3 bundles and 1 stroke. How many sparrows is that?

ask.ifNot: Count the 3 bundles in fives, then add 1 for the single stroke. That gives 16.

beats.say: 3 fives and 1 more make 16 sparrows.
Pigeons: 1 five and 4 more make 9.
Now add the three birds. 13 plus 16 is 29, and 9 more is 38.
38 birds were counted in all.
Check another way. There are 6 bundles in all, which is 30, and 8 single strokes. 30 plus 8 is 38.
A bundle is never worth 1. Count bundles in fives, then add the strokes.
A bar graph shows kites sold: Monday 14, Tuesday 9, Wednesday 17, Thursday 11. Friday's bar is twice as tall as Tuesday's. How many kites were sold on the five days?

board.text: Mon 14, Tue 9, Wed 17, Thu 11. Friday = twice Tuesday.

spec.note: Friday's bar is twice as tall as Tuesday's bar

beats.say: Friday's bar is twice as tall as Tuesday's, and Tuesday is 9. So what is Friday?

ask.ifNot: Twice as tall means 2 times as many. 2 times 9 is 18.

beats.say: 2 times 9 is 18. Friday sold 18 kites.
Now add Monday to Thursday. 14 and 11 make 25. 9 and 17 make 26. And 25 plus 26 is 51.
Don't forget Friday! 51 plus 18 is 69.
69 kites were sold altogether.
Two traps here. Twice means times 2, not plus 2. And the total needs all five days.
40 children each chose one favourite game. Cricket was chosen by 16, football by 10 and badminton by 8. All the others chose kabaddi. How many chose kabaddi?

spec.note: Cricket, football, badminton, then kabaddi

beats.say: Everyone chose one game. So the four groups together make 40, and three of the groups are known.
Add the three known groups. 16 plus 10 is 26, and 8 more is 34.
34 children chose the first three games. How many are left for kabaddi?

ask.ifNot: Take the 34 away from all 40 children. 40 minus 34 is 6.

beats.say: 40 minus 34 is 6. So 6 children chose kabaddi.
Check: 16 plus 10 plus 8 plus 6 is 40. Everyone is counted.
Add what you know, then take it away from the whole.
Meera read 12 pages on Monday, 0 pages on Tuesday, 9 on Wednesday and 15 on Thursday. What is the average number of pages she read per day?

board.text: Mon 12, Tue 0, Wed 9, Thu 15. Average per day = ?

spec.note: Average number of pages per day = ?

beats.say: The average is the fair share. If she had read the same number of pages every day, how many would that be?
First the total. 12 plus 0 plus 9 plus 15 is 36 pages.
Now we share the 36 pages over the days. On Tuesday she read nothing. So how many days do we divide by?

ask.ifNot: Tuesday is still a day, even with 0 pages. The question says four days, so we divide by 4.

beats.say: Tuesday counts. A day with 0 pages is still one of the four days. This is the trap.
36 divided by 4 is 9.
The average is 9 pages per day.
Check: 4 days of 9 pages make 36 pages. Yes. A zero still counts when you count how many.
A bar graph shows cups of tea sold: Monday 22, Tuesday 17, Wednesday 25, Thursday 19. Put the days in order from the shortest bar to the tallest bar.

board.text: Order: shortest bar to tallest bar

spec.note: Put the days in order, shortest bar to tallest

beats.say: A shorter bar means a smaller number. So we put the numbers in order, smallest first.
Which number is the smallest?

ask.ifNot: Two of the numbers have just 1 ten: 17 and 19. Of these, 17 has fewer ones. So 17 is the smallest.

beats.say: 17 is the smallest, and that is Tuesday. Next comes 19, which is Thursday.
Then 22, which is Monday. And the biggest is 25, Wednesday.
So the order is Tuesday, Thursday, Monday, Wednesday.
Watch the direction: shortest to tallest means smallest first. And do not just read the days in weekday order.
A school has three clubs. Art: 9 girls and 6 boys. Music: 7 girls and 11 boys. Chess: 5 girls and 12 boys. Which club has the most children?

board.text: Art: 9 girls, 6 boys.    Music: 7 girls, 11 boys.

spec.note: Which club has the most children?

beats.say: Most children means girls and boys together. So we add up each club.
Art: 9 plus 6 is 15.
Music has 7 girls and 11 boys. How many children is that?

ask.ifNot: 7 plus 11. First 7 plus 10 is 17, and then 1 more is 18.

beats.say: Music: 7 plus 11 is 18.
Chess: 5 plus 12 is 17.
Compare 15, 18 and 17. The biggest is 18, so the club with the most children is Music.
Art has the most girls, and Chess has the most boys. But the question asks about all the children. Add up what the question really asks for.
Children chose their favourite fruit: Mango 18, Apple 9, Banana 12, Orange 6, Grapes 3. Which fruit was chosen by exactly twice as many children as orange?

board.text: Which fruit has exactly twice as many as Orange?

spec.note: Which fruit has exactly twice as many as orange?

beats.say: Start with orange. Orange was chosen by 6 children.
What does twice as many as 6 mean?

ask.ifNot: Twice means two times. So twice as many as 6 is 2 times 6.

beats.say: 2 times 6 is 12.
Now find the fruit that 12 children chose. That is banana.
The answer is Banana.
Mango's 18 is three times 6, and Grapes' 3 is half of 6. Only banana is exactly twice.
Hardik played 5 cricket matches. His average score was 32 runs per match. How many runs did he score in the 5 matches altogether?

board.text: 5 matches. Average 32 runs per match. Total = ?

spec.note: Average 32: as if he scored 32 in each of the 5 matches

beats.say: An average of 32 means this: if he had scored the same in every match, it would be 32 each time.
So how do we get the total for the 5 matches?

ask.ifNot: The total is 5 lots of 32. Lots of means we multiply.

beats.say: 5 times 30 is 150, and 5 times 2 is 10. 150 plus 10 is 160.
Hardik scored 160 runs altogether.
Check: 160 shared over 5 matches is 32 each. So the total is the average times the number of matches.
The rainfall in a town, in millimetres, was: Monday 6, Tuesday 10, Wednesday 4, Thursday 12, Friday 8. On how many days was the rainfall more than the average?

board.text: On how many days was it more than the average?

spec.note: On how many days was the rainfall more than the average?

beats.say: There are two jobs here. First find the average. Then count the days that beat it.
Add them up: 6 plus 10 plus 4 plus 12 plus 8 is 40.
There are 5 days. 40 divided by 5 is 8. So the average is 8 millimetres.
Now compare each day with 8. Tuesday's 10 is more. Thursday's 12 is more. Monday's 6 and Wednesday's 4 are less.
What about Friday, with exactly 8?

ask.ifNot: Friday's 8 is equal to the average. Equal is not the same as more than. So Friday is left out.

beats.say: Friday is equal to the average, not more than it. So Friday is out. That is the trap.
The rainfall was more than the average on 2 days.
More than means really bigger. Find the average first, then compare with care.
Ananya's average mark in 4 tests was 18. After the 5th test, her average for all 5 tests became 20. How many marks did she get in the 5th test?

spec.note: Averages shown as equal pieces. Marks in the 5th test = ?

beats.say: Averages hide the real marks. So we turn each average into a total. A total is the average times the number of tests.
4 tests with an average of 18. 4 times 18 is 72 marks.
After 5 tests the average is 20. What is the total for all 5 tests?

ask.ifNot: Now there are 5 tests, not 4. So the total is 5 times 20, which is 100.

beats.say: 5 times 20 is 100 marks.
The total grew from 72 to 100. That jump is the 5th test. 100 minus 72 is 28.
Ananya got 28 marks in the 5th test.
Why so high? The 5th test had to score 20 for itself, and also lift each of the 4 earlier tests by 2. That is 8 extra, and 20 plus 8 is 28.
The trap is to just add 2 to 20. Always change averages into totals first.
A pictograph shows newspapers collected. Class 4A has 7 pictures and Class 4B has 4. Each picture stands for the same number. Class 4A collected 21 more than Class 4B. How many did 4A collect?

spec.note: Class 4A collected 21 more newspapers than Class 4B

beats.say: We are not told what one picture stands for. That is the puzzle. But there is a clue: the 21 more.
Class 4A has 7 pictures and 4B has 4. 7 minus 4 is 3. So 4A has 3 extra pictures.
Those 3 extra pictures are the 21 extra newspapers. So what does 1 picture stand for?

ask.ifNot: 3 pictures stand for 21 newspapers. Share 21 among the 3 pictures: 21 divided by 3 is 7.

beats.say: 21 divided by 3 is 7. Each picture stands for 7 newspapers.
Now Class 4A. It has 7 pictures, each worth 7. 7 times 7 is 49.
Class 4A collected 49 newspapers.
Check: 4B has 4 times 7, which is 28. And 49 minus 28 is 21. It fits.
When the key is missing, use the difference to find what one picture is worth.
Class 4 has 42 children, and 23 of them are girls. 15 children come to school by bus, and 9 of these are girls. How many boys do not come by bus?

board.text: 42 children, 23 girls.    15 by bus, 9 of them girls.
Boys who do NOT come by bus = ?

spec.note: How many boys do NOT come by bus?

beats.say: Lots of numbers! We want boys, so let's find out everything about the boys. First, how many boys are in the class?
42 children, and 23 are girls. 42 minus 23 is 19 boys.
15 children come by bus, and 9 of these are girls. How many boys come by bus?

ask.ifNot: The bus children are girls and boys together. Take the 9 girls away from 15, and 6 boys are left.

beats.say: 15 minus 9 is 6. So 6 boys come by bus.
There are 19 boys, and 6 of them come by bus. The rest do not. 19 minus 6 is 13.
13 boys do not come by bus.
Find all the boys, find the bus boys, then subtract. One group at a time.
Vikram found the average of five numbers to be 20. Then he saw that he had copied one number as 25 when it was really 15. What is the correct average?

board.text: Five numbers: average 20. One copied as 25, not 15.

beats.say: The average came from a total. So first find the total that Vikram used. 5 times 20 is 100.
He wrote 25, but the real number was 15. So what can we say about his total?

ask.ifNot: 25 is 10 more than 15. So he added 10 too many, and his total is 10 too big.

beats.say: 25 minus 15 is 10. His total was 10 too big, so take 10 off. 100 minus 10 is 90.
Now share the correct total among the five numbers. 90 divided by 5 is 18.
The correct average is 18.
Here is the trap: the average does not drop by 10. The 10 is shared among five numbers, so each loses 2. And 20 minus 2 is 18.
Fix the total first. Then find the average again.

A shop sold school bags: Monday 14, Tuesday 18, Wednesday 10. On Saturday it sold as many as Monday and Tuesday together. On Sunday it sold half as many as Saturday. What is the total for these five days?

board.text: Sat = Mon + Tue.    Sun = half of Sat.    Total = ?

spec.note: How many bags on these five days altogether?

beats.say: Two of the five days are hidden behind clues, so we uncover them first. Saturday is Monday and Tuesday together: 14 plus 18 is 32.
Sunday is half of Saturday. What is half of 32?

ask.ifNot: Half means divide by 2. 32 divided by 2 is 16.

beats.say: 32 divided by 2 is 16. So Sunday is 16.
Now Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday together. We already know 14 plus 18 is 32. Add Wednesday's 10 to get 42.
Add all five days. 42 plus 32 is 74, and 16 more is 90.
The shop sold 90 bags altogether.
Work out the hidden days first. Then make sure all five days are in your total.
Four friends have 8, 14, 11 and 7 marbles. They share so that all four have the same number. How many marbles must the friend who had 14 give away?

board.text: Marbles: 8, 14, 11, 7. Share so all four are equal.
How many does the friend with 14 give away?

spec.note: They share so that all four have the same number

beats.say: First we find the equal share. Put all the marbles together, then share them among the 4 friends.
8 and 7 are 15. 14 and 11 are 25. And 15 plus 25 is 40 marbles.
40 marbles among 4 friends. 40 divided by 4 is 10 each.
Is 10 the answer?

choices: no, 10 is what each ends with
ask.ifNot: 10 is the number each friend ends up with. The question asks how many the friend with 14 gives away.

beats.say: The friend with 14 must come down to 10. 14 minus 10 is 4.
That friend must give away 4 marbles.
Check: the friend with 11 gives away 1, so 5 are given away. The friend with 8 needs 2 and the friend with 7 needs 3. That is 5 needed. It balances!
Find the equal share first. Then see how far above it each friend is.
Riya's pictograph has 12 pictures, each standing for 5 stamps. Kabir's has 7 pictures, each standing for 8 stamps. Who has more stamps, and by how many?

board.text: Riya: 12 pictures of 5 stamps.  Kabir: 7 pictures of 8.
Who has more stamps, and by how many?

spec.note: Who has more stamps, and by how many?

beats.say: The two charts use different keys. So we cannot compare the pictures. We must change each chart into stamps.
Riya: 12 times 5 is 60 stamps.
Kabir has 7 pictures of 8 stamps. How many stamps is that?

ask.ifNot: 7 times 8 is 56. Here is a way to remember it: 5, 6, 7, 8. 56 is 7 times 8.

beats.say: Kabir: 7 times 8 is 56 stamps.
Riya has 60 and Kabir has 56. So Riya has more. 60 minus 56 is 4.
Riya has more stamps, by 4.
Riya has more pictures, and Kabir has bigger pictures. Only the stamps settle it. Never compare pictures from charts with different keys.
Class 4A has 20 children with an average mark of 30. Class 4B has 30 children with an average mark of 40. What is the average mark of all 50 children together?

spec.note: Average mark of all 50 children = ?

beats.say: Here is a tempting idea. The averages are 30 and 40, so just pick the middle. Is that safe?

choices: no, the classes are different sizes
ask.ifNot: The middle would be fair only if both classes were the same size. Class 4B has more children, so it pulls the average its way.

beats.say: The middle is the trap. Class 4B is bigger, so it counts for more. To be fair to every child, we use the total marks.
Class 4A: 20 children with an average of 30. 20 times 30 is 600 marks.
Class 4B: 30 children with an average of 40. 30 times 40 is 1200 marks.
Together that is 600 plus 1200, which is 1800 marks for 50 children.
Share 1800 marks among 50 children. 1800 divided by 50 is 36, because 50 times 36 is 1800.
The average mark of all 50 children is 36.
See, 36 is closer to 40 than to 30. The bigger class pulls the average towards itself. Never average two averages: go back to the totals.
On a bar graph, the bottom line stands for 20 books, not 0. Each square above it stands for 5 more books. Saturday's bar is 3 squares tall and Sunday's is 6. How many books in all?

board.text: Bottom line = 20 books. Each square above = 5 more.

spec.note: The bottom line is 20 books. Each square is 5 more books

beats.say: This graph does not start at 0. It starts at 20. So every bar already holds 20 books before we count a single square.
Saturday is 3 squares above 20. 3 times 5 is 15, and 20 plus 15 is 35.
Sunday's bar is 6 squares tall. How many books is that?

ask.ifNot: 6 squares are 6 times 5, which is 30. But the bar starts from 20, so add them: 20 plus 30 is 50.

beats.say: 6 times 5 is 30, and 20 plus 30 is 50. Sunday is 50 books.
Now both days together: 35 plus 50 is 85.
Altogether 85 books were sold.
The starting 20 belongs to each bar, so it is counted once for each day. Always check where a graph's scale begins.
In a class of 40 children, 24 like cricket and 20 like football. 6 children like neither game. How many children like both games?

board.text: 6 like neither. How many like both?

spec.note: 40 children. 6 like neither game

beats.say: First set aside the 6 who like neither game. They are on no list at all. 40 minus 6 leaves 34 children who like at least one game.
Now imagine two lists: a cricket list with 24 names and a football list with 20 names. 24 plus 20 is 44 names.
44 names, but only 34 children. How can that be?

choices: some children are on both lists
ask.ifNot: A child who likes both games is written on the cricket list and on the football list. So that child is counted twice.

beats.say: A child who likes both games is on both lists, and so is counted twice. Each such child makes 1 extra name.
How many extra names are there? 44 minus 34 is 10.
10 children like both games.
Check: cricket only is 24 minus 10, which is 14. Football only is 20 minus 10, which is 10. And 14 plus 10 plus 10 plus 6 is 40.
When two lists have more names than there are children, the extra names are the children on both lists.
The average of five whole numbers is 8. Which of the four statements on the board is certainly true?

board.text: Five whole numbers have an average of 8.
• at least one number is exactly 8
• at least one number is 8 or more
• three of the numbers are more than 8
• none of the numbers is more than 16

beats.say: Certainly true means true for every possible set of five numbers, not just for some. First, the total: 5 times 8 is 40.
To test a statement, we try to break it. One strange set does the job: 0, 0, 0, 0 and 40. It adds up to 40, so its average is 8.
In this set no number is exactly 8. Only one number is more than 8. And 40 is more than 16. So three of the statements are broken.
One statement is left: at least one number is 8 or more. Could all five numbers be less than 8?

choices: no, the total would be under 40
ask.ifNot: If every number were less than 8, five of them would add up to less than 5 times 8. But the total must be exactly 40.

beats.say: Five numbers that are each 7 or less make at most 35. That cannot reach 40. So at least one number must be 8 or more.
That is the statement that is certainly true.

board.text: At least one of the numbers is 8 or more

target.text: At least one of the numbers is 8 or more

beats.say: The numbers cannot all be below their own average. Someone has to be at the average, or above it.

Riya draws a pictograph for kites sold: Monday 12, Tuesday 18, Wednesday 30, Thursday 42. Every picture stands for the same number, only whole pictures, and as few pictures as possible. How many pictures?

board.text: Whole pictures only. Fewest pictures in all = ?

spec.note: Whole pictures only, and as few as possible

beats.say: To draw as few pictures as possible, should each picture stand for a small number of kites, or a large number?

ask.ifNot: If each picture stands for more kites, fewer pictures are needed. So we want each picture to be worth as much as possible.

beats.say: But only whole pictures are allowed. So the number for one picture must divide 12, 18, 30 and 42 exactly, with nothing left over.
Let's test. 2 divides them all. 3 divides them all. And 6 divides them all, because 12, 18, 30 and 42 are all in the 6 times table.
Can we go bigger than 6? The number must divide 12, so the only bigger one to try is 12 itself. Does 12 divide 18 exactly?

ask.ifNot: 12 goes into 18 once, with 6 left over. So 12 does not work, and 6 is the largest number that does.

beats.say: So each picture stands for 6 kites. Now the pictures for each day: 2, 3, 5 and 7.
Add the pictures. 2 plus 3 plus 5 plus 7 is 17.
Riya will draw 17 pictures altogether.
6 is only what one picture is worth. The question asks for the number of pictures. The largest key gives the fewest pictures.
A shop sold school bags: Monday 20, Tuesday 35, Wednesday 25 and Friday 40. Thursday's number is smudged, but it was exactly equal to the average of all five days. What was it?

board.text: Thursday = the average of all five days

spec.note: Thursday is exactly the average of all five days

beats.say: This sounds like a riddle. Thursday is the average, but the average needs Thursday! Here is the way in.
Think of the average as a level. If Thursday is already at that level, it pulls it neither up nor down. So the other four days must level out to the same number.

board.text: Thursday = average of the other four days

beats.say: Add the four known days. 20 plus 40 is 60, and 35 plus 25 is 60. Together that is 120.
What is the average of those four days?

ask.ifNot: There are four known days, so share 120 among 4. 120 divided by 4 is 30.

beats.say: 120 divided by 4 is 30. So Thursday should be 30.
Check with all five days. 120 plus 30 is 150, and 150 divided by 5 is 30. Thursday really is the average.
30 bags were sold on Thursday.
The trap is to divide 120 by 5. That treats Thursday as if it sold nothing. A number equal to the average leaves the average unchanged.
Riya is reading a storybook. The table shows the total pages she had read by the end of each day: Monday 12, Tuesday 30, Wednesday 41, Thursday 65, Friday 80. On which day did she read the most?

board.text: Total pages read by the end of each day:
On which day did she read the most pages?

spec.note: On which day did she read the most pages?

beats.say: Friday has the biggest number, 80. So did she read 80 pages on Friday?

choices: no, 80 is the total so far
ask.ifNot: The table shows the total pages read by the end of each day. So 80 is all five days added together, not Friday alone.

beats.say: These are running totals. To find one day's reading, take away the total of the day before.

board.text: One day = this total − the total before

beats.say: Monday is 12. Tuesday: 30 minus 12 is 18. Wednesday: 41 minus 30 is 11.
Thursday: 65 minus 41 is 24. Friday: 80 minus 65 is 15.
So day by day she read 12, 18, 11, 24 and 15 pages. The biggest is 24, and that was Thursday.
She read the most pages on Thursday.
Always read the heading of a table. Total so far is very different from pages on that day.
Kabir took five spelling tests. His average in the first three was 10. His average in the last three was 16. His average in all five was 12. What did he get in the third test?

spec.note: Marks in the third test = ?

beats.say: Three averages! Turn each one into a total. The first three tests: 3 times 10 is 30.
The last three tests: 3 times 16 is 48. All five tests: 5 times 12 is 60.
Now add the two groups: 30 plus 48 is 78. But the five tests only total 60. Something has been counted twice!
Which test is in both groups?

ask.ifNot: The first three are tests 1, 2 and 3. The last three are tests 3, 4 and 5. Test 3 is in both.

beats.say: Test 3 is in both groups. So 78 holds test 3 twice, and 60 holds it once. The difference is test 3 itself.
78 minus 60 is 18.
Kabir got 18 marks in the third test.
Check: tests 1 and 2 total 30 minus 18, which is 12. Tests 4 and 5 total 48 minus 18, which is 30. And 12 plus 18 plus 30 is 60.
When two groups overlap, add them and take away the whole. What is left is the part counted twice.
Ravi took five tests, each out of 20. In four of them he got 12, 15, 9 and 18. He forgot the fifth mark, but his average was exactly equal to one of his five marks. What is the forgotten mark?

board.text: Marks: 12, 15, 9, 18 and one forgotten (each out of 20).
The average equals one of the five marks.

beats.say: Add the four marks we know. 12 plus 18 is 30, and 15 plus 9 is 24. Together that is 54.
Here is the key idea. The average is itself a mark, so it is a whole number. That means the total of the five marks must divide exactly by 5.

board.text: Total of 5 marks must divide exactly by 5

beats.say: The total is 54 plus the forgotten mark. Which of these could the total be?

ask.ifNot: A number that divides exactly by 5 ends in 0 or in 5. Of these, only 60 does.

beats.say: The forgotten mark is between 0 and 20, so the total is between 54 and 74. The totals that divide by 5 are 55, 60, 65 and 70.
If the total is 55, the forgotten mark is 1 and the average is 11. If it is 60, the mark is 6 and the average is 12.
If it is 65, the mark is 11 and the average is 13. If it is 70, the mark is 16 and the average is 14.
The average must be one of his five marks. With averages 11, 13 and 14, no test has that mark. But 12 works: he got 12 in a test!
An average of 12 goes with a forgotten mark of 6.
When a puzzle has only a few possibilities, list them all and test each one.
Each of the 30 children in a class voted for exactly two different fruits. Mango got 20 votes, apple got 15 and banana got 14. How many votes did guava get?

board.text: 30 children. Each votes for exactly 2 fruits.

spec.note: 30 children. Each voted for two different fruits

beats.say: Before anything else: how many votes were given altogether?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 30 children gave 2 votes. So there are 2 times 30 votes, which is 60.

beats.say: 30 children with 2 votes each. 30 times 2 is 60 votes. More votes than children! That is the key.
Add the votes we know. 20 plus 15 is 35, and 14 more is 49.
The rest of the 60 votes went to guava. 60 minus 49 is 11.
Guava got 11 votes.
Check: 20 plus 15 plus 14 plus 11 is 60. All the votes are there.
The trap is to use 30 as the total. Count votes, not children, because each child voted twice.
Five different whole numbers have an average of 11. The greatest of them is 14. What is the smallest value that the smallest number could have?

board.text: Five different whole numbers. Average 11. Greatest 14.
How small can the smallest number be?

beats.say: First the total. 5 times 11 is 55. The five numbers must add up to exactly 55.
We want the smallest number to be as small as possible. So what should the other four numbers be?

ask.ifNot: The total is fixed at 55. If the other four take as much as they can, less is left over for the smallest one.

beats.say: The greatest is 14, and the numbers must all be different. So the largest four we can have are 14, 13, 12 and 11.
Add them. 14 plus 11 is 25, and 13 plus 12 is 25. Together that is 50.
What is left for the smallest number? 55 minus 50 is 5.
The smallest number could be as small as 5.
It cannot go any lower, because the other four are already as big as the rules allow.
To make one number as small as possible, make all the others as large as you can.
In Asha's pictograph each picture stands for 6 stamps. In Bina's, each stands for 4 stamps. Together they drew 22 pictures, showing 108 stamps. How many pictures did Asha draw?

board.text: Asha: 1 picture = 6 stamps.    Bina: 1 picture = 4 stamps.
22 pictures in all show 108 stamps. Asha's pictures = ?

beats.say: Here is a clever trick: pretend. Suppose all 22 pictures were Bina's kind, worth 4 stamps each. 22 times 4 is 88 stamps.
But the real total is 108, so our pretend total is too small. 108 minus 88 is 20 stamps missing.
The 20 stamps are missing because some pictures are really Asha's. Each of Asha's pictures is worth how many more than we pretended?

ask.ifNot: We counted every picture as 4, but Asha's are worth 6. 6 minus 4 is 2, so each of her pictures adds 2 more.

beats.say: Each of Asha's pictures brings 2 extra stamps, and we need 20 extra. 20 divided by 2 is 10.
Asha drew 10 pictures.
Check: Asha's 10 pictures are 60 stamps. Bina has 22 minus 10, which is 12 pictures, or 48 stamps. And 60 plus 48 is 108.
The pretend trick: suppose they are all one kind, see how far off you are, and let the gap tell you how many are the other kind.
Class 4 was asked how many pets they have. 6 children have 0 pets, 10 children have 1 pet, 2 children have 2 pets and 2 children have 3 pets. What is the average number of pets per child?

board.text: Average number of pets per child = ?

spec.note: Average number of pets per child = ?

beats.say: The average is all the pets shared among all the children. So we need two totals: the pets, and the children.

board.text: Average = all the pets ÷ all the children

beats.say: Pets first, row by row. 6 children with 0 pets give 0 pets. 10 children with 1 pet each give 10 pets.
2 children have 2 pets each. How many pets is that?

ask.ifNot: There are 2 children, and each has 2 pets. 2 times 2 is 4 pets.

beats.say: 2 times 2 is 4 pets. And 2 children with 3 pets each have 6 pets.
All the pets: 0 plus 10 plus 4 plus 6 is 20.
All the children: 6 plus 10 plus 2 plus 2 is 20.
20 pets shared among 20 children. 20 divided by 20 is 1.
The average is 1 pet per child.
Remember the 6 children with no pets. They add 0 pets, but they still count as children. Multiply across each row before you add.
Asha and Bina took the same 5 tests. Asha's average mark was 3 more than Bina's. Asha scored 85 marks altogether. How many marks did Bina score altogether?

board.text: 5 tests. Asha's average is 3 more than Bina's.

beats.say: Start with Asha's average. 85 marks over 5 tests: 85 divided by 5 is 17.
Bina's average is 3 less than that. 17 minus 3 is 14.
Is 14 the answer?

ask.ifNot: 14 is what Bina scored on average in each test. The question asks for her total over all 5 tests.

beats.say: Her total is 5 lots of 14. 5 times 14 is 70.
Bina scored 70 marks altogether.
Check the quick way: Asha leads by 3 marks in each of 5 tests. That is a lead of 15 in total, and 85 minus 15 is 70.
A gap of 3 in the average is a gap of 3 in every test. So do not just take 3 away from 85.
On a bar graph of sweets sold, Monday's bar shows 45 sweets and is 9 centimetres tall. Tuesday's bar is 4 centimetres shorter. How many sweets does Tuesday's bar show?

board.text: Tuesday's bar is 4 cm shorter. Tuesday = ? sweets

beats.say: Tuesday's bar is 4 centimetres shorter. Can we just take 4 away from 45?

ask.ifNot: The 4 is a length on the graph, in centimetres. We need to know how many sweets each centimetre stands for.

beats.say: First find what 1 centimetre stands for. 9 centimetres show 45 sweets, and 45 divided by 9 is 5.
Tuesday's bar is 4 centimetres shorter than 9. 9 minus 4 is 5, so it is 5 centimetres tall.
5 centimetres, each standing for 5 sweets. 5 times 5 is 25.
Tuesday's bar shows 25 sweets.
Check: the 4 missing centimetres are 4 times 5, which is 20 sweets. And 45 minus 20 is 25.
On a bar graph, use the scale to change heights into amounts before you add or subtract.

Each picture stands for 3 books. Asha's row has 6 pictures, Bala's has 4 and Charu's has 9. Dev's row is torn off. The four read 72 books altogether. How many more pictures did Dev's row have than Bala's?

board.text: 1 picture = 3 books. Asha 6, Bala 4, Charu 9, Dev ?

spec.note: Each picture is 3 books. 72 books altogether

beats.say: The question is about pictures. So turn the 72 books into pictures. Each picture is 3 books, and 72 divided by 3 is 24 pictures.
Count the pictures we can see. 6 plus 4 plus 9 is 19.
There are 24 pictures in all, and we can see 19. How many are in Dev's row?

ask.ifNot: Dev's row is the part that is missing. 24 minus 19 is 5 pictures.

beats.say: 24 minus 19 is 5. Dev's row had 5 pictures.
Now compare with Bala, who has 4. 5 minus 4 is 1.
Dev's row had 1 more picture than Bala's.
Take care with what is asked. Dev read 15 books, and his row had 5 pictures. But the question wants how many more pictures than Bala.
In a pictograph, one apple picture stands for 5 apples. Monday shows 3 apple pictures. How many apples were sold?

spec.note: Each picture stands for 5 apples

beats.say: The part that says one picture is 5 apples is called the key. Always read the key first.
Monday has 3 pictures, each worth 5. What do we work out?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 3 pictures stands for 5 apples. So we need 3 lots of 5, and that is 3 times 5.

beats.say: 3 times 5 is 15. Or count in fives, once for each picture: 5, 10, 15.
15 apples were sold.
3 is only the number of pictures. Use the key to turn pictures into apples.
In a bar graph, what does the tallest bar represent?

board.text: In a bar graph, the tallest bar shows ...?

beats.say: Let's make a tiny bar graph to see. Say three friends have 3, 7 and 5 stickers.
In a bar graph, each bar is drawn as tall as its number. So 3 gets a short bar, and 7 gets a tall one.
Whose bar is the tallest?

ask.ifNot: The bigger the number, the taller the bar. 7 is the biggest number, so Bina's bar is the tallest.

beats.say: Bina's bar is the tallest, because 7 is the largest number.
So the tallest bar always represents the largest value.
And the shortest bar shows the smallest value. In a bar graph, height tells you how big.
What is the mean of 12, 15, 18, 21 and 24?

spec.note: Average = ?

beats.say: Mean is another word for average, the fair share. Add all the numbers, then divide by how many there are.
Add them one at a time. 12 plus 15 is 27. Add 18 to get 45. Add 21 to get 66. And 24 more makes 90.
The total is 90. What do we divide it by?

ask.ifNot: Count the numbers: 12, 15, 18, 21, 24. There are 5 of them, so we share the total 5 ways.

beats.say: 90 divided by 5 is 18.
The mean is 18.
Here is something pretty. These numbers go up in equal steps of 3, so the mean is simply the middle one, 18.
For any mean: add everything up, then divide by how many numbers there are.
What is the mode of 3, 5, 7, 5, 9, 5, 2?
The mode is the number that appears most often. Think of it as the most popular number in the list.

board.text: Mode = the number that appears most often

beats.say: So we count how many times each number shows up. 3 appears once. 7 once. 9 once. 2 once.
How many times does 5 appear?

ask.ifNot: Point at each 5 in the list. There is one in second place, one in fourth place and one in sixth place. That is 3.

beats.say: 5 appears 3 times. That is more than any other number.
The mode is 5.
The mode is not the biggest number, and it is not the first one. It is the one you see the most.
What is the range of 14, 8, 22, 5 and 17?

spec.note: Range = ?

beats.say: The range tells us how spread out the numbers are. It is the biggest number minus the smallest.
Which are the biggest and the smallest numbers here?

ask.ifNot: Look through the whole list. Nothing is bigger than 22, and nothing is smaller than 5.

beats.say: The biggest is 22 and the smallest is 5.
22 minus 5 is 17.
The range is 17.
The range is a gap, so we subtract. Adding the biggest and the smallest is the slip to watch for.
In a pictograph, one smiley face stands for 10 students. A row shows 2 full faces and half a face. How many students is that?

board.text: 1 picture = 10 students. Row: 2 full pictures and a half.

spec.note: Each full picture stands for 10 students

beats.say: Start with the 2 full faces. 2 times 10 is 20.
Now the half face. What is it worth?

ask.ifNot: Half a picture stands for half of 10 students. Half of 10 is 5.

beats.say: Half of 10 is 5. So the half face stands for 5 students.
20 plus 5 is 25.
The row represents 25 students.
A half picture is worth half the key. Do the full pictures first, then the part picture.
Bar A shows 45 and Bar B shows 30. What is the difference?

spec.note: Difference = ?

beats.say: What does the word difference tell us to do?

ask.ifNot: The difference is the gap between two numbers. We find a gap by taking the smaller from the bigger.

beats.say: Difference means how far apart. So take the smaller from the bigger: 45 minus 30.
4 tens take away 3 tens is 1 ten, and the 5 ones stay. That is 15.
The difference is 15.
On the graph, Bar A stands 15 higher than Bar B. Check: 30 plus 15 is 45.
If you toss a coin, how likely is it that you get a head?

board.text: Toss a coin. Getting a head is ...?

beats.say: A coin has 2 sides: heads on one, tails on the other. When it lands, one of the 2 sides faces up.
Is a head certain to come up?

ask.ifNot: Certain means it happens every single time. But a coin can also land on tails.

beats.say: So a head is not certain. And it is not impossible either, because heads do come up.
The two sides are just alike. Nothing makes one side luckier than the other. So each has the same chance: 1 out of 2.

board.text: Heads: 1 out of 2.    Tails: 1 out of 2

beats.say: Getting a head is equally likely as tails.
That is why tossing a coin is a fair way to decide who goes first.
A table shows: Monday 12, Tuesday 15, Wednesday 18, Thursday 10, Friday 20. What is the total?

board.text: Mon 12, Tue 15, Wed 18, Thu 10, Fri 20. Total = ?

spec.note: Total = ?

beats.say: Five numbers to add. Don't just go from left to right. Look for friendly pairs first.
Which number pairs with 12 to make a round number?

ask.ifNot: Look at the ones digits. 2 and 8 make 10. So 12 and 18 go together to make a round number.

beats.say: 12 and 18 make 30.
10 and 20 are already round. Together they make 30 as well.
Now everything: 30 plus 30 is 60, and the 15 that is left makes 75.
The total is 75.
Pair up numbers that make tens, and tick each one off so that none is left out.
The average of 5 numbers is 20. Four of the numbers are 15, 22, 18 and 25. Find the 5th.

spec.note: Find the missing number

beats.say: If the average of 5 numbers is 20, they add up to the same as five 20s. 5 times 20 is 100.
Now add the four we know. 15 and 25 make 40. 22 and 18 make 40. Together that is 80.
The total must be 100, and four numbers make 80. So how do we find the fifth number?

ask.ifNot: The fifth number fills the gap between 80 and the full total of 100. So we subtract.

beats.say: 100 minus 80 is 20.
The fifth number is 20.
It is the same as the average! That is because the other four already average 20: 80 divided by 4 is 20.
Average times count gives the total. The missing number is the total minus the rest.
What do we call an event that will definitely happen?

board.text: An event that will definitely happen is called ...?

beats.say: In maths we have special words for how sure we are that something will happen. Let's line them up.
Impossible means it can never happen, like a cow jumping over the moon. Unlikely means it probably will not happen.
Try this one. The sun will rise tomorrow morning. How sure are we?

ask.ifNot: The sun rises every single morning. There is no doubt about it at all.

beats.say: When there is no doubt at all, and the event will definitely happen, we call it certain.
An event that will definitely happen is called certain.
Uncertain is the opposite: it means we are not sure. Definitely and certain go together.
In a pie chart, cricket takes up one quarter of the circle. What is the angle of that slice?

board.text: Cricket takes up 1/4 of the pie chart. Angle = ?

spec.note: Cricket takes up 1/4 of the circle. Angle = ?

beats.say: A pie chart is a full circle. All the way round a circle is 360 degrees.
We want one quarter of the circle. What do we do to 360?

ask.ifNot: A quarter means one of 4 equal parts. To find one of 4 equal parts, we divide by 4.

beats.say: 360 divided by 4. Half of 360 is 180, and half of 180 is 90.
The angle is 90 degrees.
90 degrees is a right angle, like the corner of a square. So a quarter slice of a pie chart always has a square corner.
Find the median of 7, 3, 9, 5 and 11.

spec.note: Median = ?

beats.say: The median is the middle number. But only after the numbers are lined up in order, from smallest to biggest.

board.text: Median = the middle number, once in order

beats.say: The list is 7, 3, 9, 5, 11. Right now the number in the middle of it is 9. So is 9 the median?

choices: no, put them in order first
ask.ifNot: The list is not in order yet. The median is the middle number only once the numbers go from smallest to biggest.

beats.say: Put them in order: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11.
Now cross off one from each end. 3 and 11 go. Then 5 and 9 go. The one left standing is 7.
The median is 7.
Order first, then find the middle. With 5 numbers, the middle one is the third.
36 books need to be shown in a pictograph. If each symbol stands for 6 books, how many symbols are needed?
Each symbol holds 6 books. So we are packing 36 books into groups of 6.
How do we find the number of groups of 6 in 36?

ask.ifNot: We want to know how many 6s fit into 36. Finding how many fit is a division.

beats.say: Count in sixes: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36. That took 6 steps. So 36 divided by 6 is 6.
6 symbols are needed.
Check by multiplying back: 6 symbols of 6 books make 36 books. To go from books to symbols, divide by the key.
A bar graph has this scale: 1 centimetre stands for 20 students. A bar is 3.5 centimetres tall. How many students does it show?

board.text: Scale: 1 cm = 20 students. The bar is 3.5 cm tall.

spec.note: 1 cm stands for 20 students

beats.say: 3.5 means 3 and a half. So split the bar into 3 whole centimetres and half a centimetre.
The 3 whole centimetres: 3 times 20 is 60 students.
And what does the half centimetre stand for?

ask.ifNot: A whole centimetre stands for 20 students. Half a centimetre stands for half of 20, which is 10.

beats.say: Half of 20 is 10.
60 plus 10 is 70.
The bar shows 70 students.
Check: 3.5 times 20 is 70. Use the scale on the whole part and on the half part, then add.
How likely is it to roll a 7 on a standard die?

board.text: Rolling a 7 on a standard die is ...?

beats.say: A standard die is a cube with 6 faces. The faces show 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.
Look at the faces. Is there a 7 anywhere?

ask.ifNot: The faces stop at 6. Read them again: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. There is no 7.

beats.say: There is no face with a 7. So however many times you roll, a 7 can never come up.
Unlikely would mean it can happen, just not often. But this can never happen at all. The word for that is impossible.
Rolling a 7 is impossible.
Before you decide how likely something is, list everything that can happen. If it is not on the list, it is impossible.
Here are ten marks: 8, 9, 8, 10, 9, 8, 7, 9, 8, 10. What is the frequency of 8?
Frequency is just a grown-up word for how many times. So we ask: how many times does the mark 8 appear?
Go along the list and ring every 8. Slowly, so that we miss none.
Count the rings. How many 8s are there?

ask.ifNot: The 8s are in first place, third place, sixth place and ninth place. That makes 4.

beats.say: There are 4 rings. So the frequency of 8 is 4.
For comparison, 9 appears 3 times and 10 appears 2 times. Mark each one as you count, so nothing is counted twice.
The average of 4 numbers is 25. Three of the numbers are 20, 30 and 22. Find the fourth.

spec.note: Find the missing number

beats.say: The average of 4 numbers is 25. What must the 4 numbers add up to?

ask.ifNot: An average of 25 means the total is the same as four 25s. 4 times 25 is 100.

beats.say: 4 times 25 is 100. The four numbers add up to 100.
Add the three we know. 20 plus 30 is 50, and 22 more is 72.
The fourth number is the rest. 100 minus 72 is 28.
The fourth number is 28.
Check: 72 plus 28 is 100, and 100 divided by 4 is 25.
Average times count gives the total. Then take away the numbers you know.
The average of 5 numbers is 60. We know 4 of them: 54, 59, 49, 54. We must find the missing one.
Here is the key. If the average of 5 numbers is 60, the numbers add up to the same as 5 lots of 60.
So how do we find the total of all 5 numbers?

ask.ifNot: If each of the 5 numbers were 60, the total would be 5 lots of 60. So we multiply.

beats.say: 60 times 5 is 300. All 5 numbers together make 300.
Now add the 4 numbers we know. 54 plus 59 is 113. Add 49 to get 162, and 54 more makes 216.
The missing number is whatever is left. 300 minus 216 is 84.
The missing number is 84.
Check: 216 plus 84 is 300, and 300 divided by 5 is 60. It works.
So: average times count gives the total. Then take away what you know.
The average of 6 numbers is 50. Then a new number, 64, joins them. What is the new average?

board.text: Average of 6 numbers is 50. A new number 64 joins.

beats.say: We do not know what the 6 numbers are. But we do not need to! Their total is enough.
6 numbers with an average of 50 add up to the same as 6 lots of 50. 50 times 6 is 300.
Now the new number joins the pot. 300 plus 64 is 364.
We must share the new total. How many numbers are there now?

ask.ifNot: There were 6 numbers, and 1 more joined. 6 plus 1 is 7. Forgetting to count the new one is the classic slip.

beats.say: There are 7 numbers now. 364 divided by 7 is 52, because 7 times 52 is 364.
The new average is 52.
The new number, 64, is bigger than the old average, 50. So it pulled the average up a little. That makes sense.
Go through the total every time. Find it, add the new number, and share it among one more.
We want the average of these five numbers: 55, 79, 65, 57, 84.
The average is the fair share. Imagine putting all the numbers into one pot, and then sharing the pot out equally.
First the total. We add one number at a time. 55 plus 79 is 134. Add 65 to get 199.
Keep going. Add 57 to get 256, and 84 more makes 340.
So the pot holds 340. How many shares do we cut it into?

ask.ifNot: Count the numbers in the list. There are 5 of them, so the total is shared 5 ways.

beats.say: 340 divided by 5 is 68, because 5 times 68 is 340.
So the average is 68.
Does it look sensible? The smallest number is 55 and the biggest is 84, and 68 sits between them. An average always does.
So for any average: add everything up, then divide by how many numbers there are.
Here are four numbers: 61, 48, 73, 62. Let's find their average.
The average is the fair share. Imagine putting all the numbers into one pot, and then sharing the pot out equally.
First the total. 61 plus 48 is 109. Add 73 to get 182, and 62 more makes 244.
So the pot holds 244. How many shares do we cut it into?

ask.ifNot: Count the numbers in the list. There are 4 of them, so the total is shared 4 ways.

beats.say: 244 divided by 4 is 61, because 4 times 61 is 244.
So the average is 61.
Does it look sensible? The smallest number is 48 and the biggest is 73, and 61 sits between them. An average always does.
Two steps every time: find the total, then share it by the count.
We want the average of these six numbers: 19, 60, 55, 42, 53, 41.
The average is the fair share. Imagine putting all the numbers into one pot, and then sharing the pot out equally.
First the total. We add one number at a time. 19 plus 60 is 79. Add 55 to get 134.
Keep going. Add 42 to get 176. Add 53 to get 229, and 41 more makes 270.
So the pot holds 270. How many shares do we cut it into?

ask.ifNot: Count the numbers in the list. There are 6 of them, so the total is shared 6 ways.

beats.say: 270 divided by 6 is 45, because 6 times 45 is 270.
So the average is 45.
Does it look sensible? The smallest number is 19 and the biggest is 60, and 45 sits between them. An average always does.
So for any average: add everything up, then divide by how many numbers there are.
